## Why we are in the room {data-menu-title="Why we are here"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-col}
[What we are]{.cell-h}

A research centre, working under an MoU with the Government of Odisha.
:::

::: {.cell-col}
[What we are selling]{.cell-h}

Nothing. No product, no licence, no fee, and no stake in any decision taken in this room.
:::

::: {.cell-col}
[What we brought]{.cell-h}

A working proof of concept, and the measurements to judge it by.
:::
:::

::: {.lead}
The specific models do not matter. Being able to tell whether any of them works is the part you cannot buy.
:::

::: notes
~60 sec, and it must come before any number. It changes how everything after it
is heard.

Say it plainly. We are not a vendor. There is nothing on sale in this room, we do
not benefit from a yes and we do not lose from a no, and that is unusual enough
in a conversation about automation that it is worth thirty seconds of your
attention.

Then the consequence, which is the actual point: because we have no stake, we
built the thing *and* measured it honestly, and the measurement is the part that
survives. Whatever the state eventually runs, whoever builds it, the question
"how would we know if this works" has to be answered by somebody with no reason
to flatter the answer.

Do not say the word vendor with any edge on it. The room may contain people with
supplier relationships and the point lands better as a description of our
position than as a warning about anyone else's.
:::

## The short version {data-menu-title="The short version"}

::: {.grid}
| | | Where it stands |
|---|---|---|
| **What automation can do** | The steps a grievance goes through before anyone can act on it | Built and measured, four components |
| **What intelligence makes possible** | What the state can *see* across a million grievances | Barely exists today. The reporting surface is resolved and pending counts |
| **How you would know** | Whether any of it, ours or anyone's, actually works | The protocol exists. Nothing has been confirmed by an officer |
:::

::: {.lead}
Automation makes each case cheaper. Intelligence changes what the state can do at all. The third one is what lets you trust either.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. Three things, and be explicit that they are not the same kind of
contribution.

Automation is the expected half. It is real, it is measured, and on its own it is
an efficiency story: the same work, done faster and more consistently.

Intelligence is the half nobody has asked for, because nobody knew it was
available. A million grievances is a continuous, self-reported, geocoded record
of what is going wrong across the state, and the system currently uses it to
count how many are closed.

The third is the one that follows from the previous slide, and it is the one to
land hardest. Everything in the first two columns will eventually be built by
somebody. The question of whether it works is separate, it is permanent, and it
needs an answer that does not come from whoever built it.

Do not give any numbers yet. The next twenty minutes are numbers.
:::

## Part 1 · What automation can do {.part data-menu-title="Part 1 · Automation"}

::: {.scorecard}
::: {.sq}
[Today]{.sc-h}

Six steps, all by hand, no record of how well any of them went.

A repeat complaint is caught when somebody happens to notice.

A grievance goes wherever cases like it went before.
:::

::: {.add}
[What is achievable]{.sc-h}

Four components, each with a time and a quality number against it.

Every one of them advisory: nothing blocks a filing, nothing assigns itself.
:::
:::

::: {.ledger}
[pipeline]{.now} [actionability]{.now} [dedup]{.now} [routing]{.now} [issues]{.off} [people]{.off}
:::

Four components on the same two axes, **time** and **performance**. Then how you
would check any of it.

::: notes
~40 sec. Signpost the structure and then hold to it rigidly: four components,
the same two questions each time, in the same table each time. How long does it
take, and how well does it do it.

The repetition is deliberate. By the third component the audience stops reading
the table's shape and reads only the numbers, which is exactly what you want by
the time you reach routing.

Say now that all four are advisory. It defuses the automation question before it
is asked, and it is true: a flag never blocks a filing, a category never assigns
itself, a route is a suggestion.

Frame the whole part as a demonstration of what is achievable rather than a
product tour, and promise the three slides at the end of it: how we measured, what
surprised us, and how to think about open versus bought. Those are the ones that
keep their value after the models are replaced.
:::

## The pipeline: reading what was filed {.add-slide data-menu-title="1 · Pipeline"}

::: {.compare}
| | Today | With this |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | 10–15 minutes to turn a petition into a complaint, self-reported [open]{.chip .chip-open} | 14 seconds for a scanned petition, under 1 second for typed text [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
| **Performance** | No measure exists for any step. Personal detail sits in the record while it is analysed | Four of the five steps now have a number. They are not equally good — see below |
| **Where it runs** | On the officer's screen, in the officer's head | Open-source models on Odisha's own hardware. No citizen text leaves, no per-call cost, no vendor lock-in [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
:::

::: {.grid}
| Step | How well it does it |
|---|---|
| Read the page | **Not separately scored.** We measure the pipeline's output, not the transcription. Today's reader is English-first; **Sarvam Vision is the planned route to Odia and handwriting** [open]{.chip .chip-open} |
| Remove personal detail | Zero mobile numbers, Aadhaar, PAN or email survived 55,544 records. 78% of hand-marked items found; over-redaction unmeasured [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
| Suggest a category | Right one in the top three 90.9% of the time, n=3,160. Top-1 is 46.6%, against labels officers say they do not invest in [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
| Draft a summary | 8 of 26 usable unedited. **The weakest component**, and not one we are asking a decision on [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
:::

::: notes
~3 min. This is four models in one row, so the second table is the slide.

First the time. Give the 14 seconds, then take it back immediately: machine
seconds are not officer minutes. The officer still reads the draft, checks it
and corrects it. What changes is what they are doing in those minutes, checking
rather than producing, and whether checking is faster has not been measured. A
poor draft is slower than no draft.

Then walk the four steps, and do not flatten them — they are genuinely of
different quality and saying so is what makes the good ones credible.

Reading the page has no score of its own. We measure what comes out of the
pipeline, not the transcription, so if someone asks how good the OCR is, the
honest answer is that we have not measured it separately.

Redaction is the strongest claim and it is the corpus scan, not the accuracy
score: shaped identifiers do not survive, checked on every record in a
district-year rather than a sample. Names are harder, 78% of what a human
marked, and over-redaction is unmeasured and has its own cost because it removes
what the officer needs.

Category is a shortlist, and it should only ever be sold as one: the right
answer is in the top three nine times in ten. Top-1 is 46.6%, and the reason
matters — officers have told us the category field does not affect routing, so
they do not invest in getting it right. We are measuring agreement with a label
nobody has an incentive to make correct.

Summary is the weakest thing we have built. Say so plainly, say we are not
asking for a decision on it, and move on. Volunteering your own worst number
before anyone finds it is worth more than the number costs.

Correct the Odia assumption here if the room holds it: officers fluent in Odia
say reading the document is not what takes the time. The constraint is
comprehension and typing, and it is the same in either language.
:::

## Watch it run {.add-slide data-menu-title="1b · Replay"}

{{< include assets/_pipeline-replay.qmd >}}

*Every stage in that bar is **open-source, on our own hardware**. Nothing leaves, nothing is metered. **Sarvam Vision is the planned route** to Odia and handwriting — hosted, so the one deliberate exception, and not a result yet.* [open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: notes
~2 min, and most of it is silence. Press Run and let it play at 1×.

Say one sentence at the start — "this is a scanned two-page Odia petition, and
the clock is the real measured timing" — and then stop talking until the bar
reaches the summary. Thirteen seconds is long enough to feel and short enough
that nobody gets restless, and the room watching a petition become a complaint
does more than any number on the previous slide.

Two things to point at when it finishes.

The shape. Two blocks carry almost all the width: reading the page and drafting
the summary. Everything between them — language, personal detail, redaction, the
review flag, category, route — is the thin strip in the middle, and together it
is under a second. So every privacy and triage control in this system is
effectively free, and if anyone wants it faster there are exactly two places to
look.

The cards. They lit up in order as each stage finished. That is the officer's
actual working material: a redacted text, a category shortlist, a route
shortlist and a draft.

Be straight about what it is if asked, and ideally before: the clock is real, the
outputs are canned, the petition was written for this slide, and no model is
running in this browser. It is a replay of a measured run, not a live demo. The
live system is on the other laptop if anyone wants to see it afterwards.

Use 4× only if you are short of time. The point is partly that 14 seconds is
genuinely quick, and `slow` is there if you want to walk the typed path stage by
stage.

THEN SWITCH TO TYPED and press Run again. It is over before you finish the
sentence: 0.13 seconds against 13.66, about a hundred times faster, and the bar
is visibly a sliver of the one before it. Two stages account for the entire
difference — there is no page to read, and this fixture ran no summary. Note the
summary card stays dark, which is honest: it did not run rather than being
hidden. Do not let it be heard as "typed complaints never get summarised"; it is
what this benchmark measured.

The operational reading, if a Secretary asks what to do with it: the expensive
path is the one citizens actually use for the hardest cases, so anything that
moves filings to typed intake, or makes the scan easier to read, pays for itself
twice.

ON THE STACK, and say this unprompted rather than waiting to be asked. Every
model in that bar is open-source and runs on hardware the state controls:
pytesseract for the page, Presidio for personal detail, MuRIL for the category,
BART for the draft. Model bytes are pinned by checksum. No citizen text leaves
the building, there is no per-call meter, and nothing in the stack can be
withdrawn, repriced or deprecated by a vendor. For a system holding a million
grievances that is a procurement and sovereignty argument as much as a technical
one, and it is the reason the whole thing runs on a laptop.

ON SARVAM, and be careful here, including about how it sits against the point
you just made: Sarvam is hosted, so adopting it would be a deliberate exception
to local-by-default, made with approval and on redacted text, and it is not in
the serving path today. Today's reader is English-first, and the measured
Odia gap is ours: the summariser skipped every coherent Odia case it was given,
through an English-only gate. Sarvam Vision is the planned route to Odia and
handwriting. It is not a result. What we have is a cached 56-page comparison in
which Sarvam extracted 1.33 times the characters, and with no hand transcription
to score against, that is a difference and not an improvement. The evidence file
says so in its own reporting rule. If asked whether Sarvam is better, the honest
answer is that we do not know yet and the test that would tell us is a
hand-transcribed set.
:::

## Actionability: what can be acted on at all {.add-slide data-menu-title="2 · Actionability"}

::: {.compare}
| | Today | With this |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | Officer judgement, made once per case, recorded nowhere | Flagged at intake with the reason named, in under a millisecond [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
| **Performance** | Unmeasurable. Nothing records what was judged or whether it was right | Caught 13 of 13 needing clarification; also sent 3 of 44 ordinary complaints to review [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} n=57 |
:::

::: {.lead}
The second number is the one that matters. It is the cost the officer pays.
:::

*Not release-eligible. 57 cases is a small test, and no officer has confirmed the labels.*

::: notes
~90 sec. The honest framing of a triage model is the false-positive rate, not
the catch rate, because the false positives are what an officer experiences.

So: it caught everything that needed clarification in its test, and it also sent
three ordinary complaints to review that did not need it. On 57 cases. Say the
denominator out loud and say that no officer has confirmed those labels, which
is the first of the four asks at the end.

Worth naming what the categories are, because it is a design choice people
approve of: it separates *underspecified*, *irrelevant*, *out of scope* and
*policy blocked* rather than calling all four spam. Those need four different
responses and only one of them is the citizen's fault.
:::

## Deduplication: counting problems, not filings {.add-slide data-menu-title="3 · Deduplication"}

::: {.compare}
| | Today | With this |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | The same problem is handled as many times as it is filed. Officers mark repeats by hand when they notice | Matched at intake, so one problem is worked once [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} 37,299 officer-confirmed repeats as the baseline |
| **Performance** | The disposal rate divides by filings, so 400 complaints about one road count 400 times | Filings, distinct problems and distinct citizens reported side by side |
:::

*How many more repeats the software finds than hand-marking does is [not yet claimed]{.chip .chip-open} — held-out recall and adjudicated precision have not been measured.*

::: {.visual}
[Visual · three descending bars]{.vtag}
Filings / distinct problems / distinct citizens for one district-year, with the
gaps between them annotated. Restyle
`docs/value-add-report/figures/fig_dedup.png` to the deck palette.
[why]{.why} The message is the *gap* between the bars. A number cannot show a gap.
[source]{.src} Demonstration slice, 55,544 redacted records.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. The road example carries this slide. A stretch of road in one block, four
hundred people file about it in a week.

Two consequences, in order of how uncomfortable they are. Operationally, four
hundred filings about one road and two hundred filings about two hundred separate
problems look identical in every report you have, and they need opposite
responses: one needs a contractor, the other needs two hundred decisions.

Then the measurement one, and judge the room before pressing it: with filings in
the denominator, a disposal percentage rises when an office attracts duplicates
and closes them. That is a property of the formula, not an accusation.

Be careful with the claim. The 37,299 are the officers' own hand-marked repeats,
so that number is theirs, not ours. What our matching adds beyond it is not
measured yet and we are not claiming it.

This slide also sets up the whole of Part 2: once you can count problems and
citizens rather than filings, you can start asking what the problems *are*.
:::

## Routing: where a grievance should go {.add-slide data-menu-title="4 · Routing"}

::: {.compare}
| | Today | With this |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | About 50 preset routes in a flat list, no default, nothing indicating which is better | No replicated gain. The apparent 2024 advantage became **−2.3 to +0.1 days** under the same augmented estimator in the untouched 2025 period [open]{.chip .chip-open} n=113,535 |
| **Performance** | The only available standard is *the same as last time*, so the best any model can do is reproduce current practice | A historical ranker is a research prototype, not a recommendation: assignment-time provenance is unresolved and no causal routing gain is established [open]{.chip .chip-open} |
:::

::: {.lead}
We changed the question. Not where do cases like this usually go, but which route actually resolves them.
:::

::: notes
~3 min. This is the most important null result in Part 1, so give it the time
the other three did not need.

Start with why the obvious version fails. If we train a model on where cases
went, the ceiling is current practice, including every bad habit in it. A
department that receives every land dispute in a district and resolves none of
them is, by that standard, exactly the right destination. That is why we are not
showing you an accuracy score for route suggestions: it would measure the wrong
thing.

Then the second row, which is the honest part. Routing purely for speed would
find the offices that *close* cases rather than the offices that *solve* them.
The 2024 development analysis appeared to show a large advantage, but the same
augmented comparison on the untouched 2025 period ranged from slightly worse to
effectively zero. The direct-model gains were not corroborated.

So: there is no day-saving claim to carry forward. The historical data also do
not prove that the recorded department is the assignment that was visible when
the decision was made, and the current actionable population is derived from
closure records rather than known at intake. Better modelling cannot repair
those missing facts.

What closes the question is prospective measurement: freeze the eligibility and
suggestion policy, record the suggestion and officer decision at assignment
time, and compare outcomes in a bounded trial. A hand-read sample can validate
the outcome proxy; it cannot estimate a routing effect on its own.
:::

## Processing, all four together {.add-slide data-menu-title="Processing summary"}

::: {.grid}
| Component | Time | Performance |
|---|---|---|
| **Pipeline** | 15 min → 14 s | Redaction: 0 shaped identifiers in 55,544. Category: 90.9% top-3. Summary: weakest, 8/26. Reading: unscored |
| **Actionability** | judgement → flagged at intake | 13/13 caught, 3/44 false, n=57 |
| **Deduplication** | handled *n* times → once | 37,299 confirmed repeats; our increment unmeasured |
| **Routing** | no replicated day-saving estimate | 2025 augmented contrast: −2.3 to +0.1 days; assignment provenance unresolved |
:::

::: {.lead}
Every row has a number. Not one of them has been confirmed by an officer.
:::

::: notes
~60 sec. Read down the middle column, then down the right, then land the line at
the bottom.

The point of showing all four at once is that the shape is consistent: each
component is faster and each has a quality number, and every quality number
rests on a test we ran on ourselves. That is the honest state of Part 1, and it
converts directly into the first ask.

Then set up the next three slides, which are the part of this section worth
keeping: "those are our numbers. The next three slides are how we got them, what
surprised us, and how you would think about buying any of this — and those
outlive whatever models anyone ends up running."
:::

## How you would check any of this {.add-slide data-menu-title="The measurement"}

::: {.lead}
The models will be replaced. The way you check them does not have to be.
:::

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| Ask of any system, including ours | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **How many cases was it tested on?** | 57 and 3,160 are different kinds of evidence, and both get called "tested" |
| **Which cases were held back and never looked at?** | A score on cases used to build the thing is not a score |
| **Were the held-back cases from a later period, or picked at random?** | Random picking lets the future leak into the past |
| **Could the same complaint sit on both sides?** | Grievances repeat. If a repeat is in both, the system is being marked on cases it has already seen |
| **How wide is the uncertainty?** | A number without a range hides how little it may rest on |
| **What result would have made you say it is not ready?** | If there is no such result, nothing was ever at risk |

:::

*Our own answer to the last one: none of what you have just seen is ready. We say so on every slide.* [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: notes
~2 min, and this is the most portable slide in the deck. Slow down.

Frame it as the thing we can give that a supplier structurally cannot. We built
these components, and we also built the test that could have failed them. Anyone
selling a system has a reason not to design that test carefully. We do not.

Walk the six questions as questions, not as our methodology. The officer should
leave able to use this list in a meeting we are not in. That is the entire point
of the slide.

The third and fourth are the ones that actually catch people, and they are worth
a sentence each. Splitting cases at random rather than by date lets a system be
tested on the same period it learned from, which flatters it. And because the
same grievance genuinely does get filed more than once, an unsplit repeat means
the system is graded on an answer it has already been given.

Then our own answer, and do not soften it: nothing here is release-eligible, we
have said so on every slide, and the last question is the one we would want asked
of us.

If anyone wants the technical version afterwards: chronological splits January to
June, July to September, October to December; exact normalised text grouped into
one split so repetitions cannot leak; Wilson intervals throughout; and the 2024
test was viewed while improving the harness, which is why we call it
developmental held-out evidence rather than a release gate.
:::

## The expensive option is not automatically the better one {.add-slide data-menu-title="What surprised us"}

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| Flagging complaints that need clarification | Large multilingual AI model | Simple word-counting method |
|---|---|---|
| **Cases needing clarification, caught** | 9 of 13 | **13 of 13** |
| **Overall accuracy** | 86% | **95%** |
:::

On 57 cases. This is a development actionability result, not a replacement for
the separate production categoriser. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: {.lead}
We are not saying simple always wins. We are saying nobody can tell you which wins on Odisha's grievances without testing both on Odisha's grievances.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. Short slide, disproportionate value, and the one most likely to be quoted
back to you later.

Tell it as a story about being wrong. We expected the large multilingual model to
win, because that is what everyone expects. In this 57-case actionability
comparison, the simple development candidate caught more of the cases needing
clarification. This does not replace the separate production categoriser.

Then the transferable point, which is the reason the slide exists. When a
proposal arrives built on a large model, the size of the model is not evidence
that it will work here. Odia, administrative vocabulary, short and messy text,
and a category list specific to this state are all things that make general
capability a poor predictor of local performance. The only thing that settles it
is a test on your own records, which is the previous slide.

Careful with the denominator and say it before anyone asks: 57 cases. It is a
small test. It is enough to say the expensive option did not automatically win;
it is not enough to say the simple one is better in general, and we are not
saying that.

Model names if anyone asks, and only if: the large actionability comparison model
was MuRIL and the simple candidate was TF-IDF. The production categoriser is a
separate model; none of those implementation details belongs on the slide.
:::

## Open, or bought {.add-slide data-menu-title="Open vs bought"}

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| | Running it yourself | Buying a hosted service |
|---|---|---|
| **Cost** | Fixed. Hardware you already own | Per call. Grows with adoption, and adoption is the goal |
| **Citizen data** | Never leaves the state's control | Leaves for processing, under whatever the contract says |
| **Capability today** | Good enough for most of the pipeline | Likely better on Odia and handwriting — we have not proven it either way [open]{.chip .chip-open} |
| **Reproducibility** | Pinned by checksum. This year's result repeats next year | The model can change behind the same name, without notice |
| **Switching** | Replace a component | Re-procure |
| **Can it be adapted to Odisha at all?** | Yes, on the state's own records | Often no. Many offerings are a fixed general model behind a prompt |
:::

::: {.asks}
[Ask in this order]{.asks-h}

**1.** Can it be adapted to our categories, our languages, our routing — at all?

**2.** If yes, who owns what our officers' corrections produce?

**3.** If no, what is the plan when it is wrong here in particular?
:::

*Not a recommendation. This is how to decide, not what to decide.* [open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: notes
~3 min. Present the table as a decision aid, not a position, and say that out
loud at the start. If pushed for a recommendation, the honest answer is that it
depends on the workload and that this table is how to decide.

Spend your time on the last row, because it is the one that is usually got
backwards. The instinctive question is "who owns the learning if the system
improves from our officers' corrections". That is a real contract question and it
should be settled before procurement rather than after — the improvement your
officers generate is either an asset of the state or an asset of the supplier,
and nobody negotiates that well afterwards.

But it is the second question, not the first. Ask first whether any adaptation is
possible at all. A great many offerings resell a general-purpose model that the
supplier cannot retrain on your data — what is on sale is a fixed model behind a
carefully written prompt. If that is what it is, "it will learn from your
officers" is not a feature that can be delivered, and the right question becomes
what happens when it is systematically wrong in a way that is specific to Odisha,
because nothing in the arrangement will fix that.

So, three questions in order: can it be adapted to our categories, our languages
and our routing at all; if yes, who owns what our officers' corrections produce;
if no, what is the plan when it is wrong here in particular.

On reproducibility, give the concrete version: a hosted model can be updated
behind a stable name, so an acceptance test passed in March may not describe what
is running in September. The mitigation is not to avoid hosted services, it is to
record what answered every call and re-run the test on a schedule — which is a
job, and it is one of the jobs the cell at the end of this talk would do.

Sarvam belongs here if it comes up: hosted, authorised under an existing
government MoU, and our planned route for Odia and handwriting. That is a
deliberate exception made with approval, not an endorsement, and we have not
proven it is better.
:::

## Part 2 · Intelligence {.part data-menu-title="Part 2 · Intelligence"}

::: {.scorecard}
::: {.sq}
[Today]{.sc-h}

Resolved and pending, counted by office and by status.

No median age, no time to resolve, no ageing.

Nothing about what the complaints are *about*, or who is making them.
:::

::: {.add}
[What is possible]{.sc-h}

**Is the system working?** How long cases take, and whether anything was done.

**What is the state learning?** Where problems are, and what is rising.

**Can anyone ask it?** A question in plain language, not a data request.
:::
:::

::: {.ledger}
[pipeline]{.on} [actionability]{.on} [dedup]{.on} [routing]{.on} [issues]{.now} [people]{.now}
:::

A million grievances is a continuous record of what is going wrong. It is
currently used to count how many are closed.

::: notes
~60 sec. Change gear here and say so. Part 1 was efficiency. This is capability.

The sentence to land: the state is already collecting a continuous,
self-reported, dated and geocoded record of what is going wrong across
thirty districts, and the only question anyone asks of it is how many are
closed. Nothing in the reporting surface asks what the complaints are about.

Three questions organise everything after this, and they are the same three that
become the cell's remit at the end. Say them now and answer them in order.

Both pips fill here. By the end of this section the ledger is complete.
:::

## What the officer sees today {.sq-slide data-menu-title="Today's reporting"}

{{< include assets/_reporting-gap.qmd >}}

Counts and a disposal percentage over filings. Nothing on the right needs new
data collection. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: {.src-line}
Verified for the CM Grievance Cell, screens reviewed 11 August 2026. Believed general; a department or Collector login has not been checked.
:::

::: notes
~90 sec. Do not rush this. It is the slide that makes the next five worth
something.

Ask the room, lightly, what the median age of a pending grievance is. Nobody
will know, because it is not on any screen. Let that sit before you touch the
arrow key.

Then step the right panel one field at a time. Each one names the column the
portal already writes, and that is the whole move: this is not a request for
new data collection, it is a request to report what is already recorded. Do not
rush the last one. `benefitted` is filled in by the closing officer, it reaches
the database, and no indicator anywhere reads it.

Say out loud that the left panel is drawn, not captured, and why: the real
screens carry citizen names and phone numbers. Saying it costs five seconds and
buys the room's trust in every other number today.

Scope it honestly and out loud rather than leaving it to the footer: we verified
this in the CM Grievance Cell. We believe it is the same product everywhere. We
have not logged into a Collector's portal, and half an hour of screen sharing
would settle it. Say the limit of your own evidence before someone else does.
:::

## Is the system working? {.add-slide data-menu-title="1 · Performance"}

::: {.compare}
| | Today | What the record already supports |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | A disposal percentage. No median age, no time to first action, no ageing | All of it, by office, subject and district, from dates already recorded [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} |
| **Quality** | Nothing. A case closed and a case solved are the same row | Whether the closing officer claimed any action at all [measured]{.chip .chip-measured} 1,209,144 closed cases |
:::

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| How 1.2M grievances were closed | Share | Median days |
|---|---|---|
| Closed claiming **no action** | 39.1% | 46 |
| Closed with wording that fits no standard category | 35.7% | 25 |
| Closed claiming **appropriate action** | 23.2% | 54 |
| Closed claiming the citizen **benefited** | 1.9% | 44 |
:::

::: {.lead}
Closing a case with action recorded takes longer than closing one without. A percentage that counts both as success cannot see that.
:::

::: notes
~3 min. This is the first of the three capabilities and it is the one officers
feel immediately. It is also the most delicate slide in the deck, so set the tone
before the numbers: this audits the existing report rather than competing with
it, and nothing here is an accusation about any office.

Time first, and it is the easy half. Every date needed to compute median age,
time to first action and ageing is already in the database. None of it is on any
screen. That is not a data problem, it is a reporting one.

Then quality, which is the half that does not exist at all today. A case that was
solved and a case that was closed with "no action possible" are the same row in
every report. Read the table slowly.

Land the last line and let it sit. Closures claiming appropriate action run at a
median of 54 days; closures claiming no action, 46. Doing the work takes longer
than not doing it, which is obvious when said aloud and invisible in a disposal
percentage. Any target built on that percentage rewards the faster of the two.

Do not present this as a discovery about officer behaviour. The wording comes
from a dropdown, the categories overlap, and a third of closures use text that
fits no standard category at all. What it establishes is narrower and stronger:
the state currently has no measure of whether anything was done, and it could
have one from records it already holds.

If asked about the benefit flag, this is the moment. Closures claiming no action
carry it more often, 9.2%, than closures claiming appropriate action, 6.2%. The
two signals disagree and in the wrong direction, which is exactly why we do not
use the flag to define whether action was taken, and why it should not be
reported as satisfaction.
:::

---

## What is the state learning? {.add-slide data-menu-title="2 · What: hotspots"}

{{< include assets/_hotspot-map.qmd >}}

All of this is in the record already. It has never been drawn. [measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: notes
~2 min, and this is the moment to slow down and let them look.

Say what they are seeing and give the denominator: 1,132,341 filings, all
thirty districts, 2021 to 2025. Every grievance carries a district and most
carry a block, so complaint intensity by place and subject is computable today,
for any category, over five years. Nothing new was collected to make this.

Read the encoding out loud once, because nobody guesses it: each dot is one
theme in one district, the colour is the theme, and the size is how many. Then
switch theme live if the room is engaged. Housing, land, police. The point lands
harder from the switching than from any single view: it is not a chart someone
made, it is a question anyone can now ask.

Two honest limits, and volunteer both rather than waiting.

A dot sits at the middle of a district, not where the complaints are. Block is
recorded on most filings and block-level dots are the obvious next version; we
have not built them because it needs boundary data we do not hold. Do not let
the dot be read as a location.

And a concentration is not automatically a problem, because a big district files
more of everything. What matters is concentration relative to what that place
normally files, which is the next slide.

If the projector cannot run it, the slide falls back to a picture of itself
automatically. Say you will send the live one round afterwards.
:::

---

## More than usual, for this place, at this time of year {.add-slide data-menu-title="2b · What is rising"}

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| The question | Why the obvious version fails |
|---|---|
| Is this more than usual **for this place**? | A big district files more of everything. Raw counts rank by population |
| More than usual **at this time of year**? | Drainage complaints rise every June. Against last month, the monsoon is an emergency every year |
| Is this **new**, or every year? | A place that complains about the same thing each year needs a different answer from one that just started |
| Is it more **people**, or more **problems**? | Four hundred citizens about one road, or two hundred separate problems. Opposite responses, identical in a count |
:::

::: {.lead}
A rise is only news against the right baseline. Three of these four are computable from the record today.
:::

*The fourth needs the repeat-matching to run across the whole corpus rather than the demonstration slice.* [open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: notes
~2.5 min. Deliberately a capability slide rather than one worked example, and
that is a decision worth understanding rather than reversing.

Two reasons. First, the honest one: the strongest rise in our data turns out to
be a week when every district and every category rose together, which is a system
event rather than a local story, and putting it up as a district finding would
invite a correction from anyone who remembers that week. Second, the useful one:
the four questions are the actual product. Any one spike is a demonstration; the
questions are what the cell would ask every week.

Walk the four as questions and let each land before the next. The second is the
one that gets nods, because everyone in the room already knows that June looks
like a crisis and is not one.

The third is worth the extra twenty seconds because people find it genuinely
interesting: chronic and acute are different problems. A place that files the
same complaint every year is a standing failure nobody has fixed. A place that
has just started is a change worth investigating now.

The fourth is the one that changes what an officer does, which is why it is last.
Say it as the road example: a stretch of road in one block, four hundred people
file in a week. That needs a contractor. Two hundred separate problems in the
same block needs two hundred decisions. Every report you have today shows those
two as the same number.

Be straight about the limit rather than burying it: separating people from
problems needs the repeat-matching running corpus-wide, and it currently runs on
the demonstration slice. Detection of the rise itself runs today.

Method names only if pressed, and only afterwards: exponentially weighted moving
average with a seasonal residual and a Poisson surprise threshold, per category
and district and week, baselined same-period-last-year, with contribution
analysis to decompose which places and subjects drove a rise.
:::

---

## Can anyone ask it a question? {.add-slide data-menu-title="3 · Ask it"}

{{< include assets/_nl-query.qmd >}}

*The answers are real, computed from the same records as the map. The understanding is canned: four fixed questions, nothing typed, no model running. Specced, not built.* [open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: notes
~2 min. The third capability, and the one that decides whether any of this gets
used by people who do not write queries.

Click through two or three presets and let the middle panel do the work. The
question goes in, the machine fills in a form, the form produces an answer. Say
plainly that today this question takes a written request to a data team and comes
back in a fortnight, if it comes back.

Be scrupulous about what is real here, and say it before anyone wonders. The
answers are genuine, computed from the same 1.1 million filings behind the map.
The understanding is not: these are four fixed questions and nothing is being
typed. Nothing is running in this browser. That distinction is exactly the
discipline the measurement slide argued for, so getting caught overstating it
here would cost more than the slide is worth.

The middle panel is worth thirty seconds because it is the design decision. The
model never writes database code. It fills in a form, and a hand-written,
tested compiler turns the form into a query. So the set of things it can ask is
bounded by construction: it cannot invent a table, cannot join something it
should not, and cannot return a number nobody can trace.

If asked why not just point a chatbot at the database, two reasons and both are
concrete. The space of legal questions across thirty districts and thirty-five
categories is combinatorial, not a list somebody can write out. And matching a
question against a bank of stored questions by similarity fails exactly where it
matters: "water complaints rising in Puri" and "water complaints falling in Puri"
look nearly identical to that kind of matching and require opposite answers.

Odia matters here and is worth saying: the intended input is a question in plain
Odia or English, not English only.
:::

## At the desk, while the officer works {.add-slide data-menu-title="What: live signal"}

::: {.deskcard}
::: {.desk-head}
Grievance intake · draft ready · <b>illustration, invented figures</b>
:::
::: {.desk-alert}
**This is the 300th complaint about water supply from Jharpada this month.**
:::
::: {.desk-body}
Same block · same category · 41 distinct citizens · first filed 3 weeks ago

Related open cases: 12 · Assigned across 3 offices
:::
:::

The same signal, delivered where a decision is being made rather than in a
monthly report. [open]{.chip .chip-open}

*Every figure on that card is invented. The components behind it exist — the
dedup grouping, the category model, the spike mart — but this assembly is a
design we have not built, and the map two slides back is real in a way this is
not.*

::: notes
~2 min. This is the slide people remember, so present the card as if it were on
the officer's screen.

The argument: everything on that card is computable from the record at the
moment the complaint is registered. None of it requires new data collection. It
is the hotspot and the spike, delivered at the desk rather than in a report
nobody opens.

Why it matters more than the dashboard: an officer registering the three
hundredth complaint about one thing does not currently know that. They process
it as a single case, because to the system it is one. The intelligence has to
arrive where the decision is, not in a monthly review.

Be clear this is a design, not a shipped feature. The components behind it exist
— dedup grouping, the category model, the spike mart — and assembling them into
this card is work we have not done. That is why it carries an estimated chip and
not a measured one. Do not let it be heard as available today.

## Who is complaining? {.add-slide data-menu-title="Who: petitioners"}

::: {.grid}
| Already in the record | What it would answer |
|---|---|
| District, block | Which places are over- and under-represented against population |
| Gender | Whether women's complaints arrive, resolve and benefit at the same rate |
| Channel — online, physical, walk-in | Who depends on paper, and whether they wait longer |
| Disability, urgency flags | Whether priority cases are actually prioritised |
:::

::: {.lead}
The interesting finding is usually who is *missing*.
:::

*Rural and urban is not a field. It would have to be derived from block against urban local body, and we have not built it.* [open]{.chip .chip-open}

::: notes
~2 min. Every field in the left column is already collected on every grievance
and none of it reaches a report.

Make the equity argument concretely rather than abstractly. A district filing far
below its population share is not a district with fewer problems. It is a
district where the grievance system is not reaching people, and that is
actionable in a way a disposal percentage never is.

The gender row is the sharpest version: we can ask not only whether women file,
but whether their complaints resolve at the same rate and carry the benefit flag
at the same rate. Nobody has asked. The data has been there since 2021.

Be straight about rural/urban since it is the obvious question: it is not a
field. Block is recorded, so it is derivable against the urban-local-body list,
and we have not built that. Marked open rather than promised.

The physical-channel row carries a real caveat worth stating: paper filings have
an unmeasured lag between receipt and registration, so their recorded wait
understates the citizen's actual wait — and Odia-language filers are
disproportionately on that channel.
:::

## Where the two questions meet: campaigns {.add-slide data-menu-title="Worked example: campaigns"}

::: {.visual}
[Visual · one campaign, both lenses]{.vtag}
Left: the issue view — the spike, with distinct problems flat while filings and
citizens climb. Right: the people view — the same event mapped, showing it
concentrated in a handful of blocks and skewed on channel.
[why]{.why} It is the one example that needs both halves of Part 2 at once, which
is exactly why it is the closing slide of the section.
[source]{.src} Campaign detection sits in `dedup`; spike labelling in `spike.py`. Use a real detected campaign, described in aggregate, never a citizen.
:::

A campaign is not a false alarm. It is many citizens organising about one real
problem — and the two lenses together are what tell you which it is.
[measured]{.chip .chip-measured}

::: notes
~2 min, and it is the payoff for the whole section.

A campaign looks like a data-quality problem to a counting system: a sudden pile
of near-identical filings, which is exactly what a naive deduplicator would
throw away. It is not noise. It is the strongest civic signal in the corpus —
many people, coordinated, about one thing they agree is wrong.

You need both questions to read it. The issue lens says filings and citizens
rose while distinct problems did not: one problem, many voices. The people lens
says where they are and how they filed. Together they distinguish a genuine
mobilisation from a deteriorating service from one aggrieved person filing
repeatedly, and those need three different responses.

This is also the honest answer to "won't dedup hide real demand?" No — because a
campaign is labelled by which of the three measures moved, and it is reported
rather than collapsed.
:::

## Part 3 · Who should own this {.part data-menu-title="Part 3 · Who owns it"}

::: {.scorecard}
::: {.sq}
[Today]{.sc-h}

Each case handled by hand, and no way to see across the million.

Performance is a disposal percentage over filings.
:::

::: {.add}
[What is possible]{.sc-h}

**Automation** makes each case cheaper and more consistent, with a number on every component.

**Intelligence** makes the corpus answer questions the state cannot currently ask.

Neither survives without somebody whose job is to check that it works.
:::
:::

::: {.ledger}
[pipeline]{.on} [actionability]{.on} [dedup]{.on} [routing]{.on} [issues]{.on} [people]{.on}
:::

::: notes
~30 sec. The ledger is full. Point at it once — this is everything that was
promised in the first minute, and each pip was shown with a number and a
limitation.

Then pose the question this part answers, and pose it as an open one: all of that
was built by a research centre that will not be here forever. Who owns it, who
runs it, and who checks it. That is the last four slides.
:::

## A Grievance Intelligence Cell {.add-slide data-menu-title="The cell"}

::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-col}
[Is the system working?]{.cell-h}

How long cases actually take, by office and subject

Whether anything was actually done, not just closed

Whether women, rural and paper filers are served equally
:::

::: {.cell-col}
[What is the state learning?]{.cell-h}

Where problems concentrate, by place and subject

What is rising more than usual for this place and season

Chronic versus new: the same complaint every year is a different problem
:::

::: {.cell-col}
[Can anyone ask it?]{.cell-h}

Questions in plain Odia or English, not a data request

Reports that assemble themselves

Answers in minutes, not a fortnight
:::

::: {.cell-col}
[Can we tell if it works?]{.cell-h}

Acceptance testing for any system, ours or a supplier's

Re-testing on a schedule, because hosted models change

Custody of the frozen cases that make any claim checkable
:::
:::

::: {.lead}
A standing capability inside government. We would help build it, support it, and independently check the fourth column.
:::

::: notes
~3 min, and this is the slide the talk has been walking towards.

Lead with why a cell and not a contract. Everything shown today is either a
capability that has to be maintained or a claim that has to be re-checked, and
both are jobs, not deliverables. A supplier can build a dashboard; nobody but the
state can own the question of whether the dashboard is telling the truth.

Take the four columns in order and keep each to about thirty seconds. The first
is the one officers feel immediately: there is currently no measure of how long
anything takes, and none at all of whether anything was actually done. The second
is what the last twenty minutes demonstrated. The third is what makes it usable
by people who do not write queries. The fourth is the one that only exists
because somebody independent is in the room, and it is the reason we are
proposing a cell rather than handing over a tool.

Be concrete about DPIC's role and bound it, because the obvious suspicion is that
we are proposing ourselves a permanent job. We would help stand it up, we would
support it, and we would independently monitor whether the automation actually
delivers. We are not asking to run it and we should not run it. The measurement
has to survive us leaving.

The full remit is wider than twelve lines: reopen rates, case-mix-adjusted office
comparison, scheme-level feedback, cross-department root cause, under-served
geographies, the definitions layer. Offer the longer list rather than putting it
on the slide, and offer to write it up.
:::

---

## What we could prove {.open-slide data-menu-title="Worth and proof"}

::: {.bignum .bignum-compact}
201,000–302,000
:::
::: {.bignum-sub}
officer-hours spent registering the 1.2M grievances already resolved — the size of the pot, not a saving [estimated]{.chip .chip-estimated}
:::

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| | Can it be proven? |
|---|---|
| Citizens wait less | Not from current records. Needs assignment-time logs and a prospective comparison |
| Where the system is not reaching people | **Yes**, today, against population |
| Fewer repeat complaints | Almost. Needs safe citizen-to-problem linkage |
| Cases reach the right office first time | Needs the suggestion-and-override log |
| Officers spend less time per case | Needs timing in the screen and a staffing figure |
| Citizens are more satisfied | No. Nothing asks them |
:::

::: {.lead}
The blocker is instrumentation and permission, not software.
:::

::: notes
~2.5 min. Two beats: the size of the prize, then what could be proven about it.

Be very careful with the big number and say why. It is arithmetic on an estimate
officers gave us. It is the denominator, not a saving, and we are claiming none
of it. It is on the slide because any future claim of time saved has to be stated
against something.

If asked what would reduce it, three things in ascending order of certainty, and
the ordering is counter-intuitive: drafting instead of typing is the largest
possible effect and the one we are least sure of, because a bad draft is slower
than no draft; handling a repeat once instead of four times is the smallest and
the one we are most sure of, because officers already recognise that work as
waste.

Then give them time to read the right-hand column before you speak. The pattern is
the argument of the whole talk: every row is blocked on something specific and
governable — a log line, an outcome-label audit, a timer in a screen, or a
prospective comparison — and not one row is blocked on a model that does not
exist. The software is the part that is nearly done.

Note the second row deliberately. Under-representation is measurable today, with
no permission and no new instrumentation, and it is arguably the highest
public-value number on this slide.

One warning to deliver here. The database records whether a petitioner benefited,
and it is tempting to report that as satisfaction. It should not be: cases closed
claiming no action carry that flag more often than cases closed claiming
appropriate action. Whatever it measures, it is not what its name suggests.
Satisfaction is something a citizen tells you, and nothing asks them.
:::

---

## The cell's first quarter {.add-slide data-menu-title="The ask"}

::: {.grid .prose-first}
| Four permissions | What it involves |
|---|---|
| **Let officers check our work** | A few officers review a fixed set of cases we have already scored |
| **Name one department for a trial** | A bounded rollout with a comparison group |
| **Log what is suggested and what the officer does** | One entry when a suggestion is shown, one when it is overridden |
| **Have ~300 closed cases read by hand** | Validates the closure-derived outcome proxy. It does not estimate routing impact by itself |
:::

::: {.lead}
None of these is a decision about automation, and none of them costs money. They are what the cell would do first.
:::

::: notes
~2 min. This is what the meeting is for. Do not hurry it and do not add to it.

Present these as a work programme rather than four favours. That is the whole
gain from the previous slide: a cell with a first quarter is a proposal, whereas
four disconnected requests are an imposition.

One: nothing shown today has been confirmed by an officer, so nothing can
responsibly be recommended for real use, and we are not recommending it.

Two: effects on officer time and on citizens cannot be worked out from
historical records. They have to be observed.

Three is the cheapest and unlocks the most. A routing suggestion already appears
on the assignment screen today, labelled as AI-suggested. Nobody knows whether
it is any good, because nothing records what officers do with it. We are not
asking to add a model. We are asking to measure the one already there.

Four: three hundred cases, about two days, to find out whether the closure-derived
outcome label means what we think it means. That audit improves the measurement;
the suggestion log and bounded trial are what can answer the routing question.

If the room wants to say yes to the cell but not yet to the four, take that. The
permissions are worth more with a cell behind them, but they stand alone and the
cell can be constituted later.

End on automation and mean it: the flag never blocks a filing, the category never
assigns itself, the route is a suggestion. Every ask here is about being able to
tell whether any of it works.
:::

---

## What we are not claiming {.open-slide data-menu-title="Not claimed"}

::: {.nonincremental}
- No officer minutes saved
- No faster resolution
- No improvement in citizen satisfaction
- No accuracy figure confirmed by an officer
:::

::: {.lead}
Everything here was measured on historical records, or on test filings on a laptop. None of it was measured in a live office.
:::

That is what the second ask would change.

::: notes
~60 sec. Close on the limits deliberately. It is unusual and it is the right note
for this room.

Not modesty — the difference between "not measured" and "measured and found to be
zero" is the entire value of a pilot, and a room that understands the difference
will grant one.

Then stop. No summary slide. The last thing on screen should be what we cannot
yet say.

Likely questions:

*"When could this be live?"* Parts run today on a laptop. Live in an office is a
decision about the trial, not about readiness.

*"What does it cost?"* The four asks cost officer time, not money.

*"Can we quote the 11 to 23 days?"* No. It was a development-period contrast
that did not replicate. The defensible sentence is: no routing gain is
established on the untouched 2025 period.

*"Is citizen data safe?"* Redaction runs before anything else. Shaped identifiers
verified absent across a district-year. Names not proven either way.

*"Can we see the map?"* Yes — and that is the best possible outcome of this talk.
:::
